action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active denervation in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles with chronic reinnervation in cervical muscles; normal conduction velocities with no conduction block at standard or proximal sites (the earlier reported block not reproduced); sensory studies normal.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No mass, brainstem lesion, demyelinating plaque, infarct or enhancing lesion; subtle corticospinal tract T2 hyperintensity and precentral low T2 signal (supportive only).
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs, including a brainstem lesion behind the new jaw jerk and palatal weakness; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal cervical and thoracic spine and cord: no compression, cord signal change or foraminal stenosis.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 842 U/L (4.8x ULN); repeat anti-GM1 IgM negative (<1:100); blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP; plus a repeat anti-GM1 IgM
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic: here a repeat anti-GM1 IgM, because the earlier MMN diagnosis rested partly on a low titre.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: WBC 1 cell/uL, protein mildly raised at 56 mg/dL (non-specific), glucose normal.
action_criteria.label: CSF only for the specific mimic question: an inflammatory motor neuropathy after the earlier MMN diagnosis
action_criteria.rationale: CSF is not part of the routine ALS work-up and does not diagnose ALS. Here the earlier immune neuropathy diagnosis raises an inflammatory neuropathy question, which the nerve conduction studies largely answer, so CSF is optional.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 74% predicted and SNIP 58 cmH2O, both reduced: inspiratory muscle weakness at baseline, without an AAN 2009 NIV marker.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic C9orf72 expansion and no pathogenic variant in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS or TBK1; a negative result does not exclude ALS.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No clinically significant interaction with amlodipine or IVIG; baseline and scheduled transaminase monitoring.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. No current medicine interacts with it.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue IVIG or start other immunotherapy as treatment for ALS.
Do not wait for FVC to fall below 50% or for respiratory symptoms before referring for NIV assessment.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive upper limb weakness, now spreading to the legs, with upper motor neuron signs (a brisk jaw jerk, brisk biceps reflexes, bilateral Hoffman signs, a left extensor plantar response and a mildly spastic gait) and lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar and cervical regions on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in thoracic and lumbosacral muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; explain why the earlier diagnosis of multifocal motor neuropathy is revised, and disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Refer to the respiratory/NIV service now because FVC (74% predicted) and SNIP (58 cmH2O) are already reduced; screen for orthopnoea and nocturnal hypoventilation with overnight oximetry or capnography, and repeat FVC and SNIP within 3 months.
Arrange a speech and language therapy assessment of speech and swallowing, with communication support, and monitor weight and swallowing at each review.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.
Stop the monthly IVIG: there is no conduction block or other evidence of an immune motor neuropathy, and IVIG has no role in ALS.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

accepted: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), previously misdiagnosed as multifocal motor neuropathy

differential.key_features: supports: the earlier diagnosis with asymmetric arm weakness, a low-titre anti-GM1 IgM (1:100) and modest early improvement on IVIG; against: upper motor neuron signs, bulbar involvement, progression despite full-dose IVIG, repeat anti-GM1 IgM negative, normal motor conduction velocities and no conduction block

supports: mildly raised CSF protein (56 mg/dL); against: normal distal latencies and conduction velocities without conduction block or temporal dispersion, normal sensory studies, upper motor neuron signs and tongue denervation
supports: CK 842 U/L (4.8x ULN); against: neurogenic EMG pattern with fibrillations, fasciculations and large polyphasic MUPs, tongue fasciculations and upper motor neuron signs
against: adult onset with no family history, upper motor neuron signs and bulbar involvement

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: a brisk jaw jerk, brisk biceps reflexes, bilateral Hoffman signs, a left extensor plantar response and a mildly spastic gait with lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar and cervical regions, with active denervation also in thoracic and lumbosacral muscles.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy or SBMA.

Multifocal motor neuropathy is a pure lower motor neuron disorder defined by motor conduction block; upper motor neuron signs, bulbar involvement and progression despite full-dose IVIG call for the diagnosis to be revisited. A low-titre anti-GM1 IgM is non-specific and is also found in ALS and other neuropathies.
CK 842 U/L (4.8x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

FVC 74% predicted and SNIP 58 cmH2O are reduced, indicating inspiratory muscle weakness. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).

findings.finding: Bilateral FDI, APB: fibrillations +2, complex fasciculation potentials, large amplitude polyphasic MUPs, severely reduced recruitment. Cervical paraspinals: fibrillations +1.

Median, ulnar, peroneal and tibial motor studies: CMAP amplitudes reduced bilaterally in the median and ulnar studies of the wasted hand muscles; distal latencies and conduction velocities normal. No conduction block at standard or proximal sites and no temporal dispersion. The possible partial conduction block reported on the study 14 months ago is not reproduced.

specialized_test.impression: Active denervation (fibrillation potentials) in the bulbar (tongue), cervical, thoracic paraspinal and lumbosacral regions, with chronic reinnervation (large amplitude polyphasic MUPs, severely reduced recruitment) in cervical muscles and fasciculation potentials in the tongue and limbs. Motor NCS show reduced CMAP amplitudes with preserved distal latencies and conduction velocities; no conduction block at standard or proximal sites. Sensory NCS normal. Findings indicate a widespread disorder of anterior horn cells.

quantitative_data.conduction_block: Absent at standard and proximal sites
quantitative_data.pattern: Active denervation in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles; chronic reinnervation in cervical muscles

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. F is a 48-year-old carpenter who was diagnosed 14 months ago with multifocal motor neuropathy based on asymmetric motor weakness, a low titer anti-GM1 antibody (1:100), and an EMG reported as showing reduced CMAP amplitudes with a possible partial motor conduction block in the forearm. He was started on monthly IVIG with initial modest improvement in grip strength over 2-3 months.

Over the past 6 months, however, his condition has steadily worsened despite continuing IVIG infusions at full dose. He has developed bilateral leg weakness that was not present at the time of diagnosis. His wife noticed tongue wasting and fasciculations, and his neurologist has documented brisk biceps reflexes bilaterally and a new left Babinski response on this visit.

His original diagnosing neurologist notes that the anti-GM1 titer was low (1:100, borderline positive in some labs) and has requested repeat evaluation at a tertiary center to reassess the original diagnosis in light of the progressive course and the new upper motor neuron findings.
